newsitem.title: USA: Stocks rebound from sell-off; bonds, dollar higher.
newsitem.headline: Stocks rebound from sell-off; bonds, dollar higher.

text.p: Blue chip stocks ended barely changed on Friday, giving the dollar a lift, as the market rebounded from a massive sell-off sparked by a profit warning from Intel Corp.
Bonds rose for the second day in a row on technical factors and hopes for moderate economic growth.
Coffee prices plummeted as profit-taking by jittery speculators ahead of the weekend took some of the air out of the most spectacular bubble in the coffee market in two decades.

The Dow Jones industrial average closed up 0.86 points to 7,331.04, reversing a sell-off that pushed the blue chip index down as much as 88 points in early trading. The Dow index fell 14.87 points for the week.
The technology-heavy Nasdaq composite index was unable to overcome the Intel hurdle, and slipped 2.72 points to 1,400.32. For the week, the Nasaq index rose 10.60 points.
"The bulls are definitely in charge," said Hildegard Zagorski, a Prudential Securities market analyst.
"The entire market is so strong, it was able to turn itself around in a broad-based rally. It's a little startling," she said.
The 30-stock blue chip average drew strength from banks and financial companies, which rallied in tandem with bonds.

Stocks tumbled at the opening after news that Intel, the world's largest maker of computer chips and a technology bellwether, said it expected its second-quarter revenues and earnings to fall short of expectations.
The news was especially shocking because Intel is known for consistenly beating Wall Street's estimates and because it came just one day after Nike Inc. said it also expected weak quarterly earnings.
After the initial scare, bargain hunters stepped in. By late trading, the Dow had crossed back into positive territory and rose about 40 points before settling back.

"The circumstances have been ripe for whippy action, so when you get a news event it can give you a sharp push up or down. But without heavier volume or broader participation, the sustainability isn't there," said Gregory Nie, technical analyst at Everen Securities.

The bond market also gave a leg up to stocks, especially banks and other financial companies. The 30-year Treasury bond rose 26/32, or $8.13 on a $1,000 bond, knocking its yield well below the psychological level of 7 percent, to 6.91 percent.
In late New York trading Friday, the dollar rose to 1.7061 German marks from 1.6965 marks late Thursday. The dollar inched up to 116.28 Japanese yen from 116.18 yen.

Coffee prices plunged as profit-taking by nervous speculators took some of the air out of the most spectacular bubble in the coffee market in two decades. At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for July delivery fell 38.40 cents a pound to close at 276.40, a decline of 12 percent in one day.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, heavy selling in palladium futures keyed a fall in precious metals.
Palladium for June delivery closed down $20.90 an ounce at $172.35, while July platinum closed down $9.10 an ounce at $401.20.
Pressured by the selloff in the platinum group, August gold at the COMEX ended down $1.10 at $347.50 an ounce and July silver down 16.3 cents at $4.675 an ounce.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybean prices closed sharply higher after a weekly report showed much stronger than expected demand from processors last week. Soybeans for July delivery closed 11 cents a bushel higher at $8.80-1/2.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 share index ended down 51.0 points at 4,621.3. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average lost 243.42 points, or 1.20 percent, to close at 20,068.81, up 59.81 from last week.
